title: A writer's Ruby: why linting should enforce your style, not a universal one
summary: DHH argues that style is an integral part of code as expression, and that Ruby's many ways to do things make it a language for writers. Linters are good when authors and teams enforce their own style, which is why Rails ships RuboCop with his omakase defaults as a starting point, not an edict.

principles.text: Style and aesthetics in code matter; the best code is its own form of poetry.
principles.quote: The best code to me is indeed its own form of poetry, and style is an integral part of such expression.

principles.text: Ruby's many ways to do things is a feature; it delights programmers who write code as authors.
principles.quote: Whereas Python’s motto has long been “there should be one – and preferably only one – obvious way to do it”, Ruby is the exact opposite.

principles.text: A universal, language-mandated style (like gofmt) is totalitarian and flattens expression.
principles.quote: That’s the most totalitarian approach. A decree on what a program should look like that’s barely two feet removed from a compile error. I don’t like that one bit.

principles.text: Linters are for authors and teams to enforce their own style on their own codebases, not to mandate style on others.
principles.quote: I think they’re excellent tools for authors and teams to enforce _their_ style with consistency on _their_ codebases.

principles.text: Rails ships a default omakase linter config as a starting point to develop your own sensibilities.
principles.quote: But it really is just a starting point for Rails programmers and teams to develop their own sensibilities, not a permanent edict on what those should be.

principles.text: Style is invariably idiosyncratic; narrowing Ruby to one pre-approved path would be a shame.
principles.quote: Ruby affords us such rich and expressive syntax that it would be a damn shame if we narrowed all possible paths down to a single, pre-approved trail.
